title: Connecting Maryland’s Past to Louisiana’s Present: The Georgetown 272
subtitle: Oral histories of the descendants of the 272 people Georgetown sold in 1838
credit: An LSU Honors College project with the T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History, LSU Libraries. Co-curated by Kaitryana M. Leinbach and Hannah N. Richards, Roger Hadfield Ogden Leaders Scholarship recipients, with Jennifer A. Cramer.
intro:
Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., is a private institution of higher education, founded as Georgetown College by the Jesuit order of the Catholic Church in 1789. In 1838, the priests administering the college sold 272 people—enslaved men, women, and children—to pay off debts and secure the school’s financial stability. They were sent to New Orleans, and then on to plantations in the Grosse Tête and Maringouin areas to labor against their will.

Long hidden by history, details of the sale were uncovered by researchers digging through the Georgetown University archives, revealing a link between Maryland’s past and Louisiana’s present. Many genealogists who seek information about their African American ancestry come to a dead end at the Civil War, for a number of reasons. Information about the Georgetown sale has proven helpful in this regard, as it has illuminated a significant trove of archival records. Hours of research have led to the identification of descendants of the Georgetown 272, many of whom still live in Louisiana.

In spring 2017 the LSU Honors College offered a course, taught by Jonathan Earle, Dean, and Jennifer A. Cramer, Director, T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History, titled “272 Slaves: Discovering Louisiana’s (and Georgetown’s) Past.” Through the course, undergraduate students learned about the history of slavery in the United States and how its legacy continues to affect us today. Students in the class conducted oral history interviews with descendants of the 272 enslaved people, members of the larger Maringouin community, and Georgetown faculty members. Two students from that class, Hannah Richards and Kaitryana Leinbach, were awarded the Roger Hadfield Ogden Leaders Scholarship to continue the work they began in class. As part of that work they conducted additional oral histories about the GU272, reviewed interviews from the 2017 class project, and co-curated this exhibition.

pages.title: Enslaved and Segregated
pages.lead_caption: Maxine Crump and Dominique Angibeau, 2017. Photo by Hannah Richards.

blocks.title: Why people didn’t pass down stories about being enslaved
blocks.bio: Maxine Crump is from Maringouin, Louisiana. She is the daughter of Emmanuel and Pauline Crump and has six siblings. Crump attended Louisiana State University in the midst of the civil rights movement and was the first African American to live in the dorms on the LSU campus. At LSU, Crump studied office administration and went on to a career in radio and television. Crump runs the Dialogue on Race Louisiana series. She is a descendant of Cornelius Hawkins, one of the 272 enslaved people sold by Georgetown, and was featured in the New York Times article that first broke the story of the discovery of living descendants. She is the vice president of the GU272 Descendants Association. By Dominique Angibeau

blocks.caption: Maxine Crump and Dominique Angibeau, 2017. Photo by Hannah Richards.

blocks.title: Why people didn’t pass down stories about being enslaved
blocks.credit: Maxine Crump, interviewed by Dominique Angibeau, 2017
blocks.transcript: They [elders] did talk about their lives. They just didn’t talk about the slave ancestry. It’s almost as if there had been a message of shame connected to having been enslaved, as if it could possibly have been their fault. It was just nothing . . . it was just something . . . My impression was that it wasn’t something to be proud of. It was more something to be ashamed of. Or I don’t know, embarrassed by it.

blocks.title: The reality of the American chattel system of slavery
blocks.bio: Mélisande Short-Colomb was born in 1954 in New Orleans, Louisiana, to St. Elmo Bauduit Short Sr. and Genevieva Wanda Lawless Short. She has one sibling, a brother thirteen years her junior. She graduated from high school and college. After twelve years as a stay-at-home mother of four, she went to culinary school, and she has worked as a professional culinarian for the past twenty years. Around July 2016, Judy Riffel of the Georgetown Memory Project contacted Short-Colomb with news of her ancestry: she is a descendant of the 272 enslaved men, women, and children sold by the Jesuits of Georgetown University. Her great-great-great-grandparents on her mother’s side, Mary Ellen Queen and Abraham Mahoney, were sold in 1838 and arrived in Louisiana aboard a ship called the Uncas. Short-Colomb has since met other descendants as they continue their genealogical research into the descendants of the 272. She takes part in genealogical seminars and studies and is a member of the GU272 Descendants Association. She now attends Georgetown University, granted legacy status. By Hannah Richards

blocks.caption: Mélisande Short-Colomb is interviewed in her Georgetown University dorm room by Hannah Richards, 2018. Photo by Kaitryana Leinbach.

blocks.title: The reality of the American chattel system of slavery
blocks.credit: Mélisande Short-Colomb, interviewed by Hannah Richards, 2018
blocks.transcript: We as descendants . . . While it is very benevolent to say we are a part of the Georgetown family, we weren’t enough family to not get sold! You know, while they were very, very concerned about our eternal souls, they really had no problem selling our physical selves. That is a reality of the American chattel system of slavery. One that we are still grappling with today as a society on the whole, and as individuals as well.

blocks.title: Growing up in Jim Crow Louisiana
blocks.bio: Carolyn Morris was born in New Orleans, Louisiana, on February 2, 1946, to Gustave and Ruth Morris. Morris moved to Plaquemine, where she began elementary school and continued her primary and secondary education. After graduating from Iberville High School, Morris began her undergraduate studies in music education at Southern University in 1963 and later received her master’s in music education at Louisiana State University. Morris then began working as an elementary music teacher in the East Baton Rouge Parish public school system. Surrounded by an underfunded music education program, Morris quickly realized she needed further certification to advance in her career. After five years as a music educator, Morris returned to LSU and received her certification in school administration. With it, Morris served as both vice principal and principal in several schools across the East Baton Rouge area for the rest of her career. After retiring, Morris was asked to return to administration, where she served at McKinley Magnet Middle School and Howell Park Elementary. Morris is married to Reginald Morris; they have three children and are retired in Zachary, Louisiana. By Rene Petit

blocks.caption: Carolyn Morris in her home in Zachary, Louisiana, 2017. Photo by Sophia Spring.

blocks.title: Growing up in Jim Crow Louisiana
blocks.credit: Carolyn Morris, interviewed by Rene Petit, 2017
blocks.transcript: [Growing up,] there were things like water fountains. Like “Black only.” “Colored only.” Or “White only.” One of the things that was very evident was that public businesses were segregated. There were businesses like Dairy Queen—sold ice cream and things like hot dogs and hamburgers, whatever. This was before Burger King and McDonald’s. Well, we couldn’t go up to the front window to purchase anything. We had to go around to the back to purchase what we needed to purchase. And even going to the doctor. If you went to a white doctor’s office, there was a white waiting room and a colored waiting room. And the colored waiting room was usually around the back of the building. You got the same . . . Paid the same price, same treatment, but you had to sit in a different place from the whites.

blocks.title: The priest who tried to integrate church seating
blocks.bio: Debra Tilson was born in Lafayette, Louisiana, on September 10, 1961, to Jessie May Fields and Burnell Poole. She grew up in Maringouin, went to Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic School, and earned her undergraduate degree from Southern University. She married and had two daughters: Mary, who died as a teenager, and Jessica, who has children of her own and remains close to her mother. Through the research of historians and genealogists, aided by the amateur genealogy of her daughter Jessica (“Millie”), Tilson discovered that she descends from one of the 272 people sold by Georgetown University to Louisiana in 1838 to help finance the institution. She works as an assessment testing coordinator at Southern and lives in Baton Rouge, though she still has a deep attachment to Maringouin and visits often. By Taylor Stirling

blocks.caption: Debra Tilson is interviewed by Taylor Stirling at Southern University, April 2017. Photo by Shaya Khorsandi.

blocks.title: The priest who tried to integrate church seating
blocks.credit: Debra Tilson, interviewed by Taylor Stirling, 2017
blocks.transcript:
And I’ll never forget there was one priest that came. And I might’ve been maybe about . . . I was in my twenties. And he came in and he saw how the church was. And he said, “Wait, before I proceed with the liturgy, the homily,” he said, “No, y’all can’t have this. I want you to get up, and I want y’all to come, y’all on this side, blacks on this side, whites . . . Look, y’all need to come together for this liturgy.” And I think he lasted about a week. [laughs] I’m serious! And after about a week or two weeks we were getting a new priest. And then everybody was back to sitting . . . But it’s just, I mean, nobody talked about it.

Even the graveyard is segregated. Whites on one side, blacks on the other side. They built this mausoleum-type deal, but it’s still like that. And if you go to the white side you not going to find the names of the . . . like Hawkins and like you find that’s on the manifest for the slaves. If you go to the white side, you not going to find those names—of the last names of the people who may or may not have gone. And that may have been because the name, last name were already given to the slaves by the time they got down here. So there is this separateness in there.

pages.lead_caption: Carolyn Morris in her home in Zachary, Louisiana, 2017. Photo by Sophia Spring.

blocks.caption: Carolyn Morris in her home in Zachary, Louisiana, 2017. Photo by Sophia Spring.

blocks.title: Sister-in-law punished for civil rights activities
blocks.credit: Carolyn Morris, interviewed by Rene Petit, 2017
blocks.transcript: Her name was Jo Ann Morris [Evelyn’s sister-in-law]. They met and decided that they would go and sit in at the Woolworth store in Baton Rouge on Third Street. And they were arrested. It was fourteen of them between a couple of places that they were sitting in. She was arrested. But not only was she arrested, the governor at the time (I think it was the governor) decided that everybody who had participated in that sit-in would be expelled or dismissed from Southern [University]. She was a freshman and she was dismissed from Southern. And they could not attend any university in the state of Louisiana. Any public university in the state of Louisiana. She ended up having to go to Central State University in Ohio, I think it is, because of her participation in the civil rights movement.

blocks.title: The attempted lynching and escape of civil rights speaker James Farmer in Plaquemine, Louisiana
blocks.bio: Tony Clayton was born on June 6, 1963. He is one of four children born to Earnest and Clara Scott Hill Clayton in Plaquemine, Louisiana. He attended Brusly High School, where he served as president of the student government. Clayton continued his education at Southern University, where he earned his B.S. in political science, and then earned his law degree at the Southern University Law Center. After law school, Clayton opened a private firm focusing on divorces, successions, and civil matters with his wife, Paula Clayton, with a large portion of his clientele coming from Iberville Parish. Clayton continues to run a private law firm, now named Clayton, Fruge, and Ward, where he made the transition from civil suits to homicide law. He is well known for his prosecution of the notorious Louisiana serial killer Derrick Todd Lee. In addition to his law practice, Clayton has served on Southern University’s Board of Advisors for twenty years. Clayton lives in Port Allen with his wife and youngest son, where he has developed a shopping center named after his late grandmother, The Village at Hun’s Grove, and owns a CC’s Coffee franchise. By RaeDiance Fuller

blocks.caption: “Vote Workers Jailed in South,” Detroit Tribune, August 24, 1963, reporting the arrest of James Farmer in Plaquemine. Chronicling America, Library of Congress.

blocks.title: The attempted lynching and escape of civil rights speaker James Farmer in Plaquemine, Louisiana
blocks.credit: Tony Clayton, interviewed by RaeDiance Fuller, 2017
blocks.transcript:
The first time CBS News came on was September the second, 1963. And what’s so relevant about that is if you Google the inaugural edition, as they’re . . . he [Walter Cronkite] starts the CBS Evening News (which is the number one news now) in Nantucket, Massachusetts, talking to then-president John Kennedy. Then he breaks the interview. At that time, he breaks back to Iberville Parish. There’s a bunch of blacks who are in a church listening to a black civil rights guy. Well, inside that church was my mom with a little kid three months old—myself. The whites roll into that church and they wanted to get Spivey Gordon, who’s the speaker. I think his name was Spivey Gordon [James Farmer]. They rode in, they beat the blacks with cattle prongs and et cetera. My uncle was in there, Clarence Hill, who’s my grandfather’s name—he’s named after. Beat the living daylights out of him. And CBS Evening News broke to that story.

Why it’s important, ultimately, they tried to get the speaker. And the black leadership back then took him and brought him to the local funeral home and put him in a hearse. Put him in a casket and drove him the only way out of Plaquemine, Louisiana. To Baton Rouge. And put him on a Greyhound bus and sent him back to Atlanta. The issue was they were looking house to house, looking for him to hang him. Because they didn’t want blacks having these civil rights folks there. The dumbness of the whites were they were checking every car, but when that hearse passed by, they took their hats off on their horses and let that hearse pass through, and unbeknownst to them, this man was in that car. In that hearse, and he got away.

blocks.title: America needs to reconcile the legacy of slavery
blocks.bio: Maxine Crump is from Maringouin, Louisiana. She is the daughter of Emmanuel and Pauline Crump and has six siblings. Crump attended Louisiana State University in the midst of the civil rights movement and was the first African American to live in the dorms on the LSU campus. At LSU, Crump studied office administration and went on to a career in radio and television. Crump runs the Dialogue on Race Louisiana series. She is a descendant of Cornelius Hawkins, one of the 272 enslaved people sold by Georgetown, and was featured in the New York Times article that first broke the story of the discovery of living descendants. She is the vice president of the GU272 Descendants Association. By Dominique Angibeau

blocks.caption: Maxine Crump gives a guest lecture to LSU and Georgetown students, 2017. Photo by Jennifer A. Cramer.

blocks.title: America needs to reconcile the legacy of slavery
blocks.credit: Maxine Crump, interviewed by Dominique Angibeau, 2017
blocks.transcript:
America just needs to wake up and recognize its slave legacy and how it is flourishing from it. This needs to become a core part of who America says it is and own this. Not just be trying to save the rest of the world, but to do whatever it takes to make life livable for those descendants of slaves. And I am a little bit sick of black people being blamed for this idea of “poor choices,” personal choices. Most of us, our ancestors didn’t even choose to come here, and now we’re hearing, “Oh, black people just make poor choices.” Well, when did these poor choices start?

So America needs to get its story straight and really, honestly, diligently do whatever it can to make sure that all of America has the fullness of what America says it is. One nation, indivisible. And we’re still divided by race. America has to fix that and stop pointing fingers at people who descended from slaves. Wrong finger-pointing. The three fingers that’s pointing back at America are the ones that need to take ownership. It needs to be at the institutional level, the government level, and all institutions that benefit and flourish. There’s no wealthy person in America that isn’t . . . that doesn’t owe part of its wealth to those who were enslaved.

blocks.caption: Mélisande Short-Colomb is interviewed in her Georgetown University dorm room, 2018. Photo by Hannah Richards.

blocks.title: The excuse that slavery was the law does not negate the damage
blocks.credit: Mélisande Short-Colomb, interviewed by Hannah Richards, 2018
blocks.transcript: I can’t pledge allegiance to a flag that has no allegiance to me. It’s pretty much that simple. I can’t say that I support a government that doesn’t support me in all of my freedoms as an American-born woman; not as a black woman. As an American woman. My oldest record . . . my oldest ancestor on record is sitting at Georgetown University, and she arrived in the United States in 1704. I ought not to be having any conversations with anybody about my Americanness and my rights as an American. It was, they say, the law of the land. Okay, it was a bad law then and it’s a bad law now, and the excuse that it was the law does not negate the damage of the law. That just gives people a pass. I’m not passing nobody.

pages.title: Growing Up
pages.lead_caption: Michelle Crump Harrington, April 6, 2017. Photo by Zoe Williamson.

blocks.title: Her parents pushed the black/white boundaries of their Catholic church
blocks.bio: Michelle Crump Harrington was born on December 17, 1964, in New Roads, Louisiana, to Emanuel and Pauline Ventress Crump. She was the youngest of seven children, so she recalls her siblings being more like parents because of the thirteen-year age gap. The family regularly attended the Catholic church of the Immaculate Heart of Mary in Maringouin, the next parish over. Mrs. Harrington attended Upper Maringouin and Thomas A. Levy for her elementary education, and then her father moved her to Catholic High in Pointe Coupee Parish, which she attended from sixth grade until her graduation. She studied communications at Southeastern for a year and a half before transferring to LSU to be closer to home. She married at nineteen and started as a part-time receptionist at what was then WRBT-TV, then worked as a temporary sales assistant, a traffic assistant, and a programming assistant before her son fell ill. She opened a hair salon with her husband and later returned to television as a program director. Mrs. Harrington and her husband have three sons, and she works as the station manager for White Knight Broadcasting in Baton Rouge. By Rainey Charbonnet

blocks.caption: Michelle Crump Harrington, April 6, 2017. Photo by Zoe Williamson.

blocks.title: Her parents pushed the black/white boundaries of their Catholic church
blocks.credit: Michelle Harrington, interviewed by Rainey Charbonnet, 2017
blocks.transcript:
We were always very close to the priest. They would always come over to eat on Sundays with us and everything. I’m glad you asked about the dynamic of the church because I always had a problem with the church. Simply because . . . And it’s still that way today: when you walk in, there’s a black side of the church and a white side of the church. My daddy was always a rebel. So we sat on the white side. And the graveyard is separated by the black side and the white side. My daddy is buried on the white side. Yeah. That’s what . . . My parents are the only two blacks buried on the opposite side of the graveyard. He just wasn’t having it. He was an activist. I don’t know how that got instilled in him to be that way, but he wasn’t having it.

I look out on the congregation, and I always wondered how can a priest look out on the congregation on a regular basis and see the people, the parishioners, divided that way and not ever speak on it? Not ever say anything. That’s why I had a problem with it. That’s why I didn’t mind going to church at school, because it wasn’t that way. I was only one of nine blacks, but still, you know, you didn’t feel like you didn’t belong. And it just felt strange.

blocks.title: Segregation in the 1990s
blocks.bio: Jessica Tilson, nicknamed Millie, was born on November 19, 1981, in Lottie, Louisiana, to Debra and Emil Tilson. She spent most of her life in Maringouin, Louisiana, before moving to Baton Rouge as a teenager. She is a mother of three. Her mother earned a degree in psychology from Southern University and is a member of its faculty. Her father is repairing their home, which was lost in the flood of summer 2016. She attended elementary school in Valverda, Louisiana, and later Livonia High School in Pointe Coupee Parish. She attended Southern University until she was twenty-one, when she left to support her daughter’s gymnastics career. She has since re-enrolled at Southern to pursue a degree in microbiology and hopes to go to law school to study medical malpractice. Tilson became interested in her family’s genealogy in the early 2000s but did not find out that she might descend from the 272 people sold by the Georgetown Jesuits until she read a 2016 newspaper article that included Maxine Crump. Tilson is working with GU272 descendants to find more of their kin and seeks to spread awareness among current and future generations of the legacy and families of enslaved African Americans. By Thailandria Daniels

blocks.caption: Jessica Tilson is interviewed by Thailandria Daniels at Southern University, 2017. Photo by RaeDiance Fuller.

blocks.title: Segregation in the 1990s
blocks.credit: Jessica Tilson, interviewed by Thailandria Daniels, 2017
blocks.transcript: The people I grew up with—we all know this. But when I talk to people on the internet, like my friends in the North, they don’t. They can’t process it when I tell them, “No. I was segregated. I wasn’t allowed to do this. And no, I wasn’t allowed to sit here.” And to them, they can’t process because we are the exact same age, and they can’t see that blacks and whites grew up like that. We still had to use the back door in the nineties when I was little. So, it’s one of those . . . it’s hard trying to explain to them, and they’re like, “What?” And me, I don’t understand how they didn’t experience that, because we all . . . all me and my friends experienced that. So why didn’t y’all experience that? So, it’s one of those . . . it’s like a culture shock, because you’re telling me you didn’t go through it, and I’m telling you that I went through it.

pages.title: Finding Out
pages.lead_caption: Mary Williams Wagner speaks with Karly Johnson, 2017. Photo by Bret Fulmer.

blocks.title: Is this really us?
blocks.bio: Mary Williams Wagner was born in Chicago, Illinois, in 1954 to Emily Elizabeth Hawkins Williams and George Williams. Her parents were born in Maringouin, Louisiana, and Cleveland, Mississippi, and they raised their fifteen children in a Catholic household. Though her parents did not attend school past the eighth grade, she attended St. Dennis Catholic School in Lockport, Illinois, where she had a happy childhood. She spent her first three years of college at Southwestern College in Kentucky studying business administration until she moved to Joliet, Illinois, for her first marriage, which resulted in two daughters. There she continued her studies at Joliet Community College, completing her four-year degree at the College of St. Francis, and became a police officer for the next twelve years. Her second marriage, to an officer in the Marine Corps, led her to Hawaii, where she joined the Oahu police department as an evidence specialist and gave birth to a son. After divorcing, she transferred to the Maui police department as the Records and Identification Section manager. She now works on the island as the information technology section’s business continuity plan manager, with a master’s in technology management. Though she did not take part in much political activism in her younger years, she is now very active in her community and the country, holding many positions in local organizations and taking part in Democratic campaigns and movements such as the Women’s March on January 21, 2017. By Karly Johnson

blocks.caption: Mary Williams Wagner speaks with Karly Johnson, 2017. Photo by Bret Fulmer.

blocks.title: Is this really us?
blocks.credit: Mary Williams Wagner, interviewed by Karly Johnson, 2017
blocks.transcript:
KARLY JOHNSON: How did you find out that you are a descendant of the GU272?

MARY WILLIAMS WAGNER: I think I found out later than some of the others. I didn’t know anything about it until, like, April of last year. So it’s only . . . It hasn’t even been a full year yet. But I found out because my brother Earle in Atlanta was sending me an email. I think he found out from another cousin. And he started sending just an email with a link in it, and it didn’t say what it was. So I ignored it the first couple times I got his email. And he would say, “Did you read the email?”

And I would say, “Mmm.”

And then he finally called and said, “Listen, you need to read this!” And so once he called, and I started reading it, I was like, well, oh my God! Oh my God, what is this? Is this really us? Because it had the direct connection of Hawkins, and you know, that was my mother’s maiden name. I knew right away that there was something there. Something real, and that this was us. As the daughter of her daughter. They were talking about us!

blocks.title: The mental and physical strength of her ancestors

blocks.caption: Elizabeth Thomas is interviewed in her New Orleans home by Hannah Richards, July 8, 2017. Photo by Kaitryana Leinbach.

blocks.title: The mental and physical strength of her ancestors
blocks.credit: Elizabeth Thomas, interviewed by Hannah Richards, 2017
blocks.transcript:
HANNAH RICHARDS: Do you think finding that you’re a direct descendant has impacted your feelings toward America’s foundation?

ELIZABETH THOMAS: No, just because I already . . . I mean. It’s my feelings like this: Every . . . I feel like almost every African American that’s in this country has some sort of an idea that “I came from slavery.” Most likely. I already had basically a knowledge that I was a descendant from slavery. And I mean, me finding this out doesn’t necessarily change how I feel about America, it just gives me more of a sense of where I come from and my past, and actually being face-to-face with, like, the horrible things my family went through. You know. It’s like finally getting the answer to a question you already knew. But once you had the answer, it’s still, like, mind-blowing.

RICHARDS: What would you like to see come out of this discovery?

THOMAS: Just finding . . . just . . . you know, more family and interconnectedness and, you know, when you just think about how mentally and physically strong these 272 people had to be, not just to make it to the country, but to stay alive while they were owned. Then to be sold and travel all the way across the country to a literally completely different part. Culturally, economically, the weather—the whole scene is different. And how mentally and physically strong they had to be, and the bond they had to have together to stay alive with each other. The human connection part of it.

blocks.title: “I’m more American than you!”
blocks.credit: Jessica Tilson, interviewed by Thailandria Daniels, 2017
blocks.transcript:
THAILANDRIA DANIELS: So how did you feel about that initially? Finding out that you were a descendant?

JESSICA TILSON: I was happy, because most black people . . . I mean, you can’t get past 1895, and here we are, 1770. What! You have a paper trail, which most of us . . . we don’t have a paper trail. You just hear stories. So here I am, a black person. Black black. Here I am. I have my ancestry dating to the American Revolution. That was the most exciting thing ever, because I used to tell my white friends, “I’m more American than you! Your family came in the 1800s and I was already here.” You know. It’s like a sense of . . . I wouldn’t know exactly what part of Africa I’m from, but I’m past that hurdle that most blacks can’t make, that connection with that one slave. And here I am. It’s just so many of them. It’s like ecstatic.

pages.title: Jesuits and Georgetown
pages.lead_caption: Clara Ann Clayton, 2017. Photo by Russell Wilder.

blocks.title: The frustration of not knowing your history
blocks.bio: Clara Ann Clayton was born on December 16, 1941, to Mr. Clarence Hill and Mrs. Lucia Scott Hill and is the second oldest of five children. Her family lived in Vallejo, California, until her mother passed away when Clayton was only four. Her maternal grandmother, Mrs. Clara Gay Scott, took the children back to Plaquemine, Louisiana, where she raised the oldest four, and Clayton’s father and his mother raised the youngest. Clayton attended trade school before getting her degree in nursing. A little while after marrying her husband, Clayton moved to Port Allen, Louisiana, in 1964, where she still lives. When she was little, Clayton attended church at St. Peter Baptist Church in Plaquemine as well as her aunt’s church, Grace Methodist Church. Clayton is a direct descendant of Isaac Hawkins. A widowed housewife, Clayton has four children and several grandchildren. She is a member of several Masonic societies, including the Eastern Star and the Daughters. In her free time, she travels with the Red Hatters across the country to see historical monuments and cities. By Russell Wilder

blocks.caption: Clara Ann Clayton, 2017. Photo by Russell Wilder.

blocks.title: The frustration of not knowing your history
blocks.credit: Clara Ann Clayton, interviewed by Russell Wilder, 2017
blocks.transcript:
RUSSELL WILDER: What do you know about the Georgetown sale of the 272 slaves? Outside of the family tree. How does it make you feel?

CLARA ANN CLAYTON: To be honest, it’s kind of . . . I hate to say . . . You don’t want to say hate. But it just give you a bad feeling to know this is what happened. But then it’s not just the Georgetown. I mean, this was worldwide. It was everywhere. But the slaves that they were selling them—you hate knowing that. Okay, this is a Christian institute, that they would do something like that. But then I try not to be angry, because that’s life. But sometime when you think about it, you just get . . . I’m fixing to say pissed, but [laughs] you get . . . you really kind of just get angry. But I mean, the older you get, you just come to: Okay, that’s life. This is what happens. Nothing you can do about it.

Now that’s really . . . That’s irritating, because you cannot go back. I can’t go back and say, “Okay, I know where my people . . . my great-great-grandfathers and stuff come from,” because I really don’t. You just have to kind of shake it off and go on.

blocks.title: Looking for acknowledgment, not apologies
blocks.bio: Michelle Crump Harrington was born on December 17, 1964, in New Roads, Louisiana, to Emanuel and Pauline Ventress Crump. She was the youngest of seven children, so she recalls her siblings being more like parents because of the thirteen-year age gap. The family regularly attended the Catholic church of the Immaculate Heart of Mary in Maringouin, the next parish over. Mrs. Harrington attended Upper Maringouin and Thomas A. Levy for her elementary education, and then her father moved her to Catholic High in Pointe Coupee Parish, which she attended from sixth grade until her graduation. She studied communications at Southeastern for a year and a half before transferring to LSU to be closer to home. She married at nineteen and started as a part-time receptionist at what was then WRBT-TV, then worked as a temporary sales assistant, a traffic assistant, and a programming assistant before her son fell ill. She opened a hair salon with her husband and later returned to television as a program director. Mrs. Harrington and her husband have three sons, and she works as the station manager for White Knight Broadcasting in Baton Rouge. By Rainey Charbonnet

blocks.caption: Michelle Harrington is interviewed by Rainey Charbonnet at her home in Baton Rouge, April 6, 2017. Photo by Zoe Williamson.

blocks.title: Looking for acknowledgment, not apologies
blocks.credit: Michelle Harrington, interviewed by Rainey Charbonnet, 2017
blocks.transcript:
RAINEY CHARBONNET: How do you feel about Georgetown’s decision to rename one of their buildings for Isaac Hawkins?

MICHELLE HARRINGTON: It’s the happiest thing. That was one of the things I asked for when the president came. Because he asked, “What would you like us to do?”

I said, “I’d like a family reunion [laughs] sponsored by Georgetown.” And I said, “And I’d like for there to be some sort of remembrance or dedication for our ancestors.” Being a dedication, dedicating a building, or just an area where you go for peace and solitude, or just something in their honor. That’s all I wanted. It’s my understanding that part of what’s going to happen on the eighteenth is there’s going to be an official apology. It is what it is at that point. That’s not what I’m looking for. I’d rather there’d be just acknowledgment. Acknowledgment that it was wrong, and that we know better now. When you know better you do better.

blocks.title: A sense of betrayal by the Catholic Jesuits
blocks.bio: Mary Williams Wagner was born in Chicago, Illinois, in 1954 to Emily Elizabeth Hawkins Williams and George Williams. Her parents were born in Maringouin, Louisiana, and Cleveland, Mississippi, and they raised their fifteen children in a Catholic household. Though her parents did not attend school past the eighth grade, she attended St. Dennis Catholic School in Lockport, Illinois, where she had a happy childhood. She spent her first three years of college at Southwestern College in Kentucky studying business administration until she moved to Joliet, Illinois, for her first marriage, which resulted in two daughters. There she continued her studies at Joliet Community College, completing her four-year degree at the College of St. Francis, and became a police officer for the next twelve years. Her second marriage, to an officer in the Marine Corps, led her to Hawaii, where she joined the Oahu police department as an evidence specialist and gave birth to a son. After divorcing, she transferred to the Maui police department as the Records and Identification Section manager. She now works on the island as the information technology section’s business continuity plan manager, with a master’s in technology management. Though she did not take part in much political activism in her younger years, she is now very active in her community and the country, holding many positions in local organizations and taking part in Democratic campaigns and movements such as the Women’s March on January 21, 2017. By Karly Johnson

blocks.caption: Mary Williams Wagner speaks with Karly Johnson, 2017. Photo by Bret Fulmer.

blocks.title: A sense of betrayal by the Catholic Jesuits
blocks.credit: Mary Williams Wagner, interviewed by Karly Johnson, 2017
blocks.transcript: Shocked. And there’s a sense of betrayal too. To learn that it was Catholic Jesuit priests that were involved in this instead of providing sanctuary. They were engaging in this practice of human trafficking, is really what it amounts to. Profiting off of another human is what they engaged in. And you know, growing up as a Catholic it was like—how could they do that? And you know, doesn’t that violate all of the tenets of the Catholic Church and what you know about it, or what we knew about it as young people growing up with the Catholic Church? It was shocking. It was disturbing, and it kind of rocks the center of your core, because [of] who you think you are. And then you discover that it’s something different, or something more than that.

blocks.title: A dark part of our history
blocks.bio: Rashaad Jackson was born on December 23, 1980, in New Orleans, Louisiana, to Katherine Jackson (née Coleman) and Richard S. Jackson. He has two older sisters, Gina Washington and Anika Jackson. In New Orleans, Jackson attended the New Orleans Center for Science and Mathematics, where he expanded his passion for math and science. After high school, he continued his education at the University of Southern Mississippi in Hattiesburg. After a negative experience there, Jackson spent a semester at the University of New Orleans. He then transferred to Southern University in Baton Rouge, where he finished his degree in computer science. At Southern, Jackson was a member of the football team for a semester, and he was also a member of the National Quiz Bowl team, the National Court Appointed Special Advocate Association, and the College Democrats. Jackson works at Louisiana State University as a Systems and Network Administrator 3 with Residential Life. By Staci Shelby

blocks.caption: Rashaad Jackson is interviewed by Staci Shelby at LSU, April 5, 2017. Photo by Tia Jones.

blocks.title: A dark part of our history
blocks.credit: Rashaad Jackson, interviewed by Staci Shelby, April 5, 2017
blocks.transcript: The Jesuits are a specific group, and then the Georgetown Jesuits are a subgroup of them, right? And it’s not like the order came down from the Pope to sell the slaves. And if I’m not mistaken, the church in general was not happy about it after it happened. So you have that. But too, you have to remember that Baptist churches, Protestant churches of all denominations, nonreligious people all sold and bought human chattel. It is a dark part of our history that we’ll probably never fully address because, why? Because it would make people feel bad and better. So, not happy about it—the sale, or really slavery in general, especially the way it was conducted in the United States.

blocks.title: Involve descendants in what reconciliation looks like
blocks.bio: Karran Harper Royal was born on August 2, 1963, and lived with her mother and stepfather. She grew up in the New Orleans projects and graduated from Warren Easton High School. During her senior year, her brother, who had Batten disease, a terminal illness, passed away. Her mother divorced that same year, so Royal worked several jobs to help support her family and wasn’t able to attend college. She worked her way up in retail management while marrying and raising two sons. She eventually quit her job to focus on her son’s special education, which his school was neglecting, and she became a special education advocate in New Orleans from 1992 until 2016. Since finding out her family’s connection to the Georgetown sale of 272 enslaved people, she has been heavily involved in creating the GU272 Descendants Association and serves as its executive director. She works tirelessly to reconnect the families torn apart by the sale. By Shaya Khorsandi

blocks.caption: Karran Harper Royal, 2018.

blocks.body:
Karran Harper Royal, interviewed by Hannah Richards, 2018. Recording not found.

We would like to be able to be collaborative in our relationship and efforts with the school, the Society of Jesus, and the Pope. I’m talking about future plans for what reconciliation really looks like, because they only have one half of the equation, and that’s the Georgetown perspective. Whether it’s Georgetown students and faculty and the Jesuits. But they did not have the descendants’ perspective on what reconciliation looks like. And that work still needs to be done.

pages.title: Future Hopes
pages.lead_caption: Adam Rothman is interviewed in his office by Kaitryana Leinbach, 2018. Photo by Hannah Richards.

blocks.title: How can we look with new eyes at our own deeds?
blocks.bio:
Adam Rothman is a professor in the History Department at Georgetown University. He studies the history of the United States from the Revolution to the Civil War, and the history of slavery and abolition in the Atlantic world. He teaches undergraduate and graduate courses in Atlantic history, nineteenth-century U.S. history, and the history of slavery.

His most recent book is Beyond Freedom’s Reach: A Kidnapping in the Twilight of Slavery (Harvard University Press, 2015), which was named a Humanities Book of the Year by the Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities and has received the Jefferson Davis Book Award from the American Civil War Museum and the Margaret T. Lane/Virginia F. Saunders Memorial Research Award from the Government Documents Round Table of the American Library Association. Rothman served on Georgetown’s Working Group on Slavery, Memory, and Reconciliation in 2015–2016 and is the principal curator of the Georgetown Slavery Archive.

blocks.caption: Adam Rothman is interviewed in his office by Kaitryana Leinbach, 2018. Photo by Hannah Richards.

blocks.title: How can we look with new eyes at our own deeds?
blocks.credit: Adam Rothman, interviewed by Kaitryana Leinbach, 2018
blocks.transcript:
KAITRYANA LEINBACH: So, in an ideal world, what would you hope to come out of the findings and the research and the new light shed on this?

ADAM ROTHMAN: I think there are two things: one is a really positive and constructive collaboration between Georgetown and the Jesuits and the descendant community to help advance educational and economic opportunities for members of the descendant community who are in need. That’s one thing.

The second thing is there’s a deeper question here: What is history good for? Why do we study history at all? Ultimately, I think one of the reasons we study history is to learn, but what do we learn? One thing we learn is that we need to try to broaden our moral imagination. So you look at what happened in 1838, and the Jesuits were operating within a very limited moral universe where they cared more about the financial stability of the university and the order than the lives of this group of people. They basically sacrificed that group of people for their own interest. If you look at the history like that, it’s a horrible history. A very traumatic history. But rather than just say, “Those are bad people and they did a bad thing,” I think it should cause us to look at ourselves and think, “Well, what are we doing—who are we sacrificing for our own interests, and how can we look with new eyes at our own deeds?” So, I guess, ultimately, thinking and learning about this history should be able to make us more aware of our own morality.

blocks.title: We all ought to put some skin in the game
blocks.bio: Tony Clayton was born on June 6, 1963. He is one of four children born to Earnest and Clara Scott Hill Clayton in Plaquemine, Louisiana. He attended Brusly High School, where he served as president of the student government. Clayton continued his education at Southern University, where he earned his B.S. in political science, and then earned his law degree at the Southern University Law Center. After law school, Clayton opened a private firm focusing on divorces, successions, and civil matters with his wife, Paula Clayton, with a large portion of his clientele coming from Iberville Parish. Clayton continues to run a private law firm, now named Clayton, Fruge, and Ward, where he made the transition from civil suits to homicide law. He is well known for his prosecution of the notorious Louisiana serial killer Derrick Todd Lee. In addition to his law practice, Clayton has served on Southern University’s Board of Advisors for twenty years. Clayton lives in Port Allen with his wife and youngest son, where he has developed a shopping center named after his late grandmother, The Village at Hun’s Grove, and owns a CC’s Coffee franchise. By RaeDiance Fuller

blocks.caption: Tony Clayton in his home office, 2017. Photo by RaeDiance Fuller.

blocks.title: We all ought to put some skin in the game
blocks.credit: Tony Clayton, interviewed by RaeDiance Fuller, 2017
blocks.transcript:
You may not like this, but I’m going to say it anyway. I’m somewhat offended by the heirs looking for some type of reparation. Suing for a billion dollars. I think that’s ridiculous. I think it’s not rooted in any substance or logic or common sense. Because slavery was legal back at the time they sold my great-great-great-great-great-grandfather. So therefore, there’s no recourse, because it was the law of the land. Do I subscribe to and support that? Absolutely not. But you can’t sue with that. I think it’s a missed opportunity with my newfound relatives, that they are misguided in their venture.

The trajectory of this new relationship should be one of creating a bond, creating a relationship with Georgetown so that kids like me can go and get educated there. I think Isaac Hawkins’ relatives who have somewhat worked hard and made it, I think we all . . . we all, and quote me on this, ought to put some skin in the game with this. Because it’s about helping that kid who’s less fortunate than the rest of us. Let’s put together a big pot, create something here. So that kids who look like me, and out of all 272, can have an opportunity to get this so-called Ivy League education that emanated from Georgetown University.

blocks.title: Outreach should include educational opportunities
blocks.bio: Mélisande Short-Colomb was born in 1954 in New Orleans, Louisiana, to St. Elmo Bauduit Short Sr. and Genevieva Wanda Lawless Short. She has one sibling, a brother thirteen years her junior. She graduated from high school and college. After twelve years as a stay-at-home mother of four, she went to culinary school, and she has worked as a professional culinarian for the past twenty years. Around July 2016, Judy Riffel of the Georgetown Memory Project contacted Short-Colomb with news of her ancestry: she is a descendant of the 272 enslaved men, women, and children sold by the Jesuits of Georgetown University. Her great-great-great-grandparents on her mother’s side, Mary Ellen Queen and Abraham Mahoney, were sold in 1838 and arrived in Louisiana aboard a ship called the Uncas. Short-Colomb has since met other descendants as they continue their genealogical research into the descendants of the 272. She takes part in genealogical seminars and studies and is a member of the GU272 Descendants Association. She now attends Georgetown University, granted legacy status. By Hannah Richards

blocks.caption: Mélisande Short-Colomb is interviewed in her Georgetown University dorm room, January 19, 2018. Photo by Hannah Richards.

blocks.title: Outreach should include educational opportunities
blocks.credit: Mélisande Short-Colomb, interviewed by Hannah Richards, 2018
blocks.transcript: Sure. I would like to see the Jesuits do a bit more outreach in descendant communities, especially communities where there are large concentrations of descendants. Let’s start building those relationships and educational opportunities for those children as well. What is a reparation? Is it money in a person’s hand, or is it value in kind? Nobody could give me enough money for me to come here and [be] paid to do this. I would like to see this opportunity [to attend university] within the framework of what the Jesuits do. They provide great education across the country, and the world. So, within the framework of what they do, in terms of suspended tuition in high schools, in elementary schools, partnering to raise funds with descendant groups. Can anybody pay me for my family and them being sold? No. There’s no money for that. I can’t even factor that into a dollar amount. For me.

blocks.title: We need to open up critical research into where we are going as a nation
blocks.bio: Leroy Baker was born in 1954 in New Orleans, Louisiana, to Marian and Ronald Baker. He is the great-great-great-grandson of Nace and Biby Butler, sold by the Jesuit priest Thomas F. Mulledy to Jesse Batey of Terrebonne Parish. Lee worked for his father at their 24-hour restaurant even after his parents filed for divorce. After he finished high school, he enrolled at St. Joseph Seminary College to pursue the priesthood. Baker was the first African American allowed in the New Orleans Athletic Club, in the 1980s. He spent most of his working career as a program director for Covenant House. Lee is in his sixteenth year of teaching theology at Archbishop Rummel High School and will soon start teaching at Tulane University. He found out at a 2004 family reunion that he is related to two of the original GU272. By Bret Fulmer

blocks.caption: Dr. Ibrahima Seck gives LSU and Georgetown students a tour of Whitney Plantation, 2017. Photo by Jennifer A. Cramer.

blocks.title: We need to open up critical research into where we are going as a nation
blocks.credit: Leroy Baker, interviewed by Bret Fulmer, 2017
blocks.transcript:
As I understand it, this aspect of history is not taught, and also history from the enslaved perspective is not taught enough in school. And other aspects of not just slavery, as you can see. I talk about desegregation and the battle of that all the way until the ’80s and ’90s. A lot of folks think that after 1865, “Oh, Lincoln freed the slaves. Hallelujah.” We had a few moments of Reconstruction, and after that, this whole Jim Crow, KKK-era intimidation. It was hell. That’s not taught in school. They kind of skim over that. We took hell. And I was always amazed at how my folks were able to not only buy property at the time of Plessy v. Ferguson in 1898, but hold on into the time of Jim Crow, when African Americans were being lynched and everything else. We’re being disenfranchised once again from this country. And that lasted . . . the legacy lasted until recent times.

I think hopefully we can open up for critical research and development where we have come from and where we are going as a nation. That’s what my hope is. Whether it’s LSU, I think, in part that too. Other levels, higher ed, high school, elementary education. So that we continue to grow and expand who we are as human beings and also citizens of these United States.

blocks.title: Involve descendants in research and education about the GU272
blocks.bio: Leroy Baker was born in 1954 in New Orleans, Louisiana, to Marian and Ronald Baker. He is the great-great-great-grandson of Nace and Biby Butler, sold by the Jesuit priest Thomas F. Mulledy to Jesse Batey of Terrebonne Parish. Lee worked for his father at their 24-hour restaurant even after his parents filed for divorce. After he finished high school, he enrolled at St. Joseph Seminary College to pursue the priesthood. Baker was the first African American allowed in the New Orleans Athletic Club, in the 1980s. He spent most of his working career as a program director for Covenant House. Lee is in his sixteenth year of teaching theology at Archbishop Rummel High School and will soon start teaching at Tulane University. He found out at a 2004 family reunion that he is related to two of the original GU272. By Bret Fulmer

blocks.caption: Rev. Leroy Baker and Onita Estes-Hicks at Georgetown University, April 18, 2017. Photo by Adelle M. Banks, Religion News Service.

blocks.title: Involve descendants in research and education about the GU272
blocks.credit: Leroy Baker, interviewed by Bret Fulmer, 2017
blocks.transcript:
I’m just one person out of 10,000 descendants. I want them just to keep the process of listening to create just that. What I discovered in communicating with the administration at the president’s office, in particular, that there were other descendants that, of course, I wasn’t privy to knowing that they existed or they were communicating with them. And I stumbled on that. So we made sure that everybody who was known to be a representative of a group had something so that . . . Hey, you a part of this and you a valued member. So, the transparency—let us communicate with us about what’s going on. In fact, who are the descendants? So that we can communicate with each other. Unless somebody says, “Hey, for privacy reasons, they don’t want anybody else to know.”

Also, there’s got to be ways that Georgetown and the Jesuits can find ways to almost create opportunities for capacity. What I mean by that, say with research and archives, that we’re not coming always to them. We have people who are PhDs, graduate students, and the like who could really participate in some of the research, too. In fact, they are. We are, in terms of . . . Also, a lot of things related to the GU272, we can be a part of, lecturing and developing other academic and nonacademic programs related to GU272. In addition to, obviously, that there were other things, in fact, that the descendants spoke about at the gathering on last Tuesday. That list is kind of extensive. But I think the openness, the transparency, and they’re willing to say, “Hey. Receive us as people worthy of being included,” is the beginning.

blocks.title: This learning experience
blocks.bio: Jessica Tilson, nicknamed Millie, was born on November 19, 1981, in Lottie, Louisiana, to Debra and Emil Tilson. She spent most of her life in Maringouin, Louisiana, before moving to Baton Rouge as a teenager. She is a mother of three. Her mother earned a degree in psychology from Southern University and is a member of its faculty. Her father is repairing their home, which was lost in the flood of summer 2016. She attended elementary school in Valverda, Louisiana, and later Livonia High School in Pointe Coupee Parish. She attended Southern University until she was twenty-one, when she left to support her daughter’s gymnastics career. She has since re-enrolled at Southern to pursue a degree in microbiology and hopes to go to law school to study medical malpractice. Tilson became interested in her family’s genealogy in the early 2000s but did not find out that she might descend from the 272 people sold by the Georgetown Jesuits until she read a 2016 newspaper article that included Maxine Crump. Tilson is working with GU272 descendants to find more of their kin and seeks to spread awareness among current and future generations of the legacy and families of enslaved African Americans. By Thailandria Daniels

blocks.caption: Jessica Tilson and Jonathan Earle, dean of the LSU Honors College.

blocks.title: This learning experience
blocks.credit: Jessica Tilson, interviewed by Thailandria Daniels, 2017
blocks.transcript:
THAILANDRIA DANIELS: So how do you feel now? Like, through all this, throughout this process, how do you feel at this moment, right now? [background noise of river barge traffic]

JESSICA TILSON: I feel great, because I’ve learned so much. Not about just my family, but I have traced families that I’m not related to. And I know that a baby died in childbirth. You know, it’s one of those . . . it feels good when I know that certain . . . I know some people died from suicide. I know cholera was bad. They had malaria out here. You know, it’s one of those things I didn’t know, like they were teaching slaves how to read. All my life I kept hearing that slaves were not allowed to learn how to read. So, some places they built schools. They gave them ceremonies. They let them do certain things, which goes against those, the movies that I watched. So, I feel great. I hope other people will go out and look and help a friend or whatever with your ancestors. Like I tell people, it doesn’t have to be your family. You can just sit on a census record, pick a name, and try to find that person.

blocks.body:
“The purpose of this project is to shed light on a history that has gone unnoticed or unheard, in a journey that has only begun. We’ve interviewed people with a story to tell, from the Georgetown 272 descendants to professors at Georgetown University. All of our interviewees play a significant role in the connections we’ve made of past to present.

We would like to thank the Roger Hadfield Ogden Honors College for the funding for this project. Special thanks to Jennifer Cramer and the T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History for making this project possible.”

Co-curators Kaitryana M. Leinbach and Hannah N. Richards, Roger Hadfield Ogden Leaders Scholarship recipients

Acknowledgments

The listening station portion of the exhibition was co-curated by Hannah Richards and Kaitryana Leinbach, LSU Honors College students. Oversight and content contributions by Jennifer A. Cramer, Director, T. Harry Williams Center for Oral History. Additional content selection by Taylor Stirling, Center Student Assistant. Audio engineered by Anne Wheeler and Chandler Taylor, Center Graduate Assistants. The gallery and online listening station interface was designed and installed by Kyle Tanglao, User Interface Designer, Technology Initiatives, LSU Libraries.

The curators wish to thank Leah W. Jewett, Exhibitions Coordinator; and Russell Wilder, Alexis Baptiste, and Cindy Sonbuchner, Williams Center Student Assistants, for their assistance. The curators also thank LSU Honors College Dean Jonathan Earle, the students of the Spring 2017 Honors 2030 class, and the narrators who shared their stories.

More narrators

The narrators’ biographies were written by the students who interviewed them, as their final project in the Honors 2030 class, 2017. These narrators were also interviewed for the project.

Evelyn Georgetown Pugh

Evelyn Georgetown Pugh, a descendant of one of the 272 enslaved people sold by Georgetown in 1838, was born to Osborn Georgetown and Clore Williams Georgetown on May 17, 1932, in Plaquemine, Louisiana, where her parents sharecropped on rented land. She attended segregated schools through the eighth grade and later returned to earn her GED. She held many jobs throughout her life: first she sold grave gowns to funeral homes, and later she began a catering business that included baking wedding cakes. She is a devout Baptist; growing up she attended church every Sunday and still does today. She had five children and adopted three others through the foster care system with her husband. Although her children have scattered across the country, she still lives in Plaquemine.

Delores Johnson

Delores Johnson was born in 1950 in Chicago, Illinois, to George Williams and Emily Elizabeth Hawkins Williams. Her father was from Cleveland, Mississippi, and her mother from Maringouin, Louisiana. The couple met in Chicago while George was working for a railroad company and Emily was visiting the city. Johnson grew up in Lockport, Illinois, just outside Chicago, and now lives in University Park, Illinois. Her family was the only African American family in Lockport that had been Catholic since birth, and Johnson and her siblings all attended Catholic elementary school. She attended a Catholic high school for her freshman year before transferring. Johnson has no memories of her grandparents, who died before she was born, while her parents were both young. Now retired, Johnson worked as a bookkeeper for a nonprofit organization and later as an office manager for a forestry service. She is working with her sister Mary and others on the discovery of descendants of the 272 people sold from Georgetown University by Jesuit priests to Louisiana. Johnson has several children and grandchildren. By Scarlett Hammond

Ethel Murphy

Ethel Murphy was born on May 10, 1937, in Maringouin, Louisiana, the thirteenth of nineteen children born to Ben Poole and Elnora Hicks Poole. She lived in Maringouin until she was sixteen and attended an African American elementary and middle school. At sixteen, she moved to St. Louis to live with her older brother. Murphy didn’t continue in high school, and she worked various jobs, most significantly at two hospitals. While in St. Louis, she married a man in the military and moved to California for a short time, then divorced at twenty-one and returned to Maringouin, where she has remained. She married again and had two sons, and she now has grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Murphy worked at Louisiana State University for twenty years, ending her career there as the kitchen supervisor in Pleasant Hall, then an on-campus hotel. In the 1990s, Murphy received her GED from Shady Brook High School in Maringouin. She works at a doctor’s office in Baton Rouge twice a week and still lives in Maringouin with her younger son. By Sophia Spring

Bernadine Poole

Bernadine Poole was born on September 6, 1966, in New Roads, Louisiana, to Jessie May Fields Poole and John Burnell Poole. She has lived in Maringouin, Louisiana, since birth. Poole attended Head Start in a building that has since become a bar, elementary school at Upper Maringouin School, and T. A. Levy High School. She was the third person in her family to attend college, and she graduated from Southern University in Baton Rouge with a degree in computer science. Poole attended Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic Church growing up and still does today. She spent most of her childhood summers at her grandmother’s house, playing outdoors with her cousins and neighbors. Poole became very involved, alongside her niece Jessica, in researching her lineage and its ties to the Georgetown 272. She took a DNA test to discover her mother’s family, since she already knew a lot about her father’s ancestors. Poole is an IT Support Specialist 2 at the State of Louisiana Office of Technology Services. She lives with her father, John Burnell Poole. By Zoe Williamson
